gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many watt-hours these '3,000 Wh' stations actually deliver when a lab measures them. Notebookcheck measured about 2,650 Wh from the BLUETTI Elite 300 and about 2,500 Wh from the Anker SOLIX F3000, both at a load of roughly 200 W. StorageReview measured 2.39 kWh from the BLUETTI Apex 300, 2.67 kWh from the Elite 300 and 2.61 kWh from the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra Plus.
standout_why: I compared against the StormWatts kit comparison, which is cited in both chats (dated 2026-11-08, updated 2026-11-12). It says outright 'We have not tested these products hands-on.' Its capacities are maker ratings. Its only efficiency figure is an assumed 0.85, and its only measurement is one solar-input reading by the unnamed site owner on a different station, the Explorer 2000 Plus. It gives no delivered Wh, no round-trip efficiency and no idle draw for any 3 kWh kit. The other cited rival, unpluggedwatts.com, would not open: WebFetch failed on a self-signed certificate, and curl through Bash needed approval I did not have. I could not check whether it has measured figures, so the score assumes it does not. The uncited top results were not opened.
decides: The finding mostly confirms the pick and partly changes it. In the same lab under the same ~200 W load (Notebookcheck, Marcus Schwarten), the Elite 300, rated 3,014.4 Wh, delivered about 2,650 Wh. The Anker F3000, rated 3,072 Wh, delivered about 2,500 Wh. At StorageReview the Elite 300 delivered 2.67 kWh and the Apex 300 delivered 2.39 kWh. So the BLUETTI Elite 300 + 2×200 W kit (link price $1,614.05, pre-order dispatching late November 2026) gives more measured usable energy than the Apex 300 + 2×200 W kit ($2,089.05, pre-order dispatching late January 2027) for $475 less. That works out to about $609 per measured kWh against about $874. It probably also gives more than the F3000 kit at 200 W loads. The trade-off is AC output: 2,400 W on the Elite 300 against 3,600–3,840 W on the others. At 1,800 W, Notebookcheck measured almost 2,800 Wh (91%) from the F3000 and just over 92% from the Elite 300. These figures do not decide the ship-now pick, because I found no lab measurement for the ALLPOWERS R3500, our only ship-now kit in this size (R3500 + SP037 400 W, and R3500 + SP039 600 W). For a shopper who keeps the station plugged in on standby, The Solar Lab measured 8 W idle on the Jackery HomePower 3000 against about 20–22 W on the F3000, Apex 300 and DELTA 3 Ultra.

findings.label: Measured AC energy delivered, low load (Notebookcheck)
findings.source_title: 3 kWh in a compact package: Powerstation Bluetti Elite 300 review (Notebookcheck)
findings.note: Marcus Schwarten, published 2026-03-09, updated 2026-10-05. Constant load of just over 200 W. At 1,800 W the efficiency was 'just over 92%' (no Wh given; 0.92 × 3,014.4 ≈ 2,773 Wh is my arithmetic). AC charging at 1,200 W drew 3,450 Wh, about 87% reaching the battery. Noise was over 50 dB at 1 m under load. EU unit tested.

findings.label: Measured discharge and recharge (StorageReview)
findings.value: 2.67 kWh delivered; 3.49 kWh to recharge from 0–100%; UPS switchover 8 ms line-to-battery
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 300 Review: 3014Wh, 2400W and an 8ms UPS Switchover in a 58-Pound Box
findings.note: Dylan Bryan, 2026-08-27. Discharge load wattage not stated. My arithmetic: 2.67 / 3.0144 = 88.6% of rated, and 2.67 / 3.49 = 76.5% round trip. Battery-back-to-line switchover was 8.25 ms.

findings.label: Measured discharge, recharge and UPS (StorageReview)
findings.value: 2.39 kWh delivered (86% of 2,764.8 Wh); 3.30 kWh to recharge; about 72% round trip; UPS 16 ms
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Apex 300 Review: 3840W, 240V, Grid Input Limit, UPS (StorageReview)
findings.note: Kevin OBrien, 2026-11-09. Load was a large blower fan, a steady inductive load of unstated wattage. The 16 ms switchover was captured with a Quarch analyzer in 120 V (20 ms) mode at about 100 W and about 700 W. An Apex 300 with 2× B300K delivered 7.38 kWh (89%).

Wall charge 0–80% took 89 min at 1,800 W.
